notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Timothy 1. I ran out of searches before covering everything, so a few verses have little or nothing. Those gaps are listed at the end. Enduring Word (David Guzik) is summarised without tagged citations because that page came back as plain text. It cuts off partway through v. 8.

---

**Background: who wrote the letter**
- *Traditional view:* Paul wrote 2 Timothy from prison during his second Roman imprisonment (ca. A.D. 66–67), shortly before his death. https://bible.org/seriespage/introduction-27 . Another bible.org writer believes "the evidence is on the side of Pauline authorship, with the help of an amanuensis (perhaps Luke)." https://bible.org/seriespage/16-2-timothy-introduction-argument-and-outline
- *Modern scholarship (as reported by these sites):* Scholars often cite the Pastoral Epistles as pseudonymous (written under Paul's name by someone else) because their language differs so markedly from Paul's undisputed letters. https://au.thegospelcoalition.org/article/did-paul-really-write-this-letter/ . An older dictionary says many critics hold that the letters contain genuine fragments of the Apostle's writing, but their present form is the work of pseudonymous writers. It answers that the argument from 'style' is a most precarious one. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hdb/t/timothy-epistles-to.html
- *Catholic:* The older Catholic Encyclopedia argues that the case against Paul presented more difficulties than the Pauline case. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/epistles-to-timothy-and-titus

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Paul is an apostle by God's will, not by his own ambition or human choice. "The promise of life" doesn't appear in his other greetings. It fits here because Paul is back in prison in Rome expecting execution, which gives the letter its urgency. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/

**v. 2**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon. Paul's letters to churches open with "grace and peace," but his letters to the pastors Timothy and Titus add "mercy." Spurgeon took this to mean ministers need more mercy than others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/
- Precept Austin quotes Towner: "God's unearnable love and peace will overshadow his servant even in the most difficult of circumstances." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59625/

**v. 3**
- Precept Austin: Paul wanted Timothy to know he suffered because of his faithfulness to the Lord, not because of ungodly living. Near death, his conscience did not accuse him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_13-4
- Guzik: Paul kept Timothy on his prayer list. When he couldn't preach, he prayed. Guzik also reads "forefathers" as the Jews before Paul who truly followed God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/

**v. 4**
- Guzik suggests the tears may have been the ones Timothy shed when they last parted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/

**v. 5**
- Guzik: Timothy's faith owed much to his grandmother and mother. His father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). Even so, the faith had to be Timothy's own. "Sincere" literally means "unhypocritical," a faith that isn't an act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/
- GotQuestions: Lois and Eunice likely taught him the Jewish Scriptures. https://www.gotquestions.org/spirit-of-fear.html
- Precept Austin quotes Lenski: Paul considers it a model, the standard he measures other people's faith against. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_15-7

**v. 6 (a verse where traditions really differ)**
- *What "fan into flame" means:* Pulpit Commentary: the verb appears here only in the New Testament, but found in the LXX, the Greek Old Testament, meaning "to revive." There it follows despondency or fear. https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/1-6.htm . Precept Austin stresses the present tense: Timothy is to keep the flame blazing as he has been doing. This is not a rebuke for neglect but a fatherly appeal; it is preventative rather than corrective. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_15-7 . Gill, by contrast, thinks there seems as if there was some decline, some backwardness and indifference. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-6.html
- *Reformed:* Calvin: the excellence of gifts produces carelessness, accompanied by sloth; and Satan continually labors to extinguish all that is of God in us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-6.html . Calvin admits some doubt whether the laying on of hands means ordination, since spiritual gifts were given to many who weren't pastors. Still, he concludes from 1 Timothy 4:14 that Paul here speaks of the office of a pastor. https://www.ccel.org/study/2_Timothy_1:6-7
- *Methodist/Wesleyan:* Adam Clarke: The gift which Timothy had received was the Holy Spirit; and through him, a particular power to preach and defend the truth. He adds that only apostles could give the Holy Spirit, and that Timothy was afterwards ordained by the presbytery. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-6.html
- *Restoration Movement:* Coffman sees the gift as an office: the office Timothy held as an apostolic representative. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-6.html
- *Pentecostal/charismatic-leaning:* Guzik says God used the laying on of hands to pass spiritual gifts to Timothy. It is a common way God gives gifts and should not be neglected, so we should ask others to pray for gifts for us. He also warns against passively waiting for some dramatic new anointing when God is waiting for us to stir up what we already have. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/ . Chuck Smith links it to prophecy: the gift Timothy received when the hands were laid upon you and the gift of prophecy was exercised. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-6.html
- *Evangelical:* GotQuestions thinks the gift was most likely the gift of pastoral administration or the gift of preaching. It says Paul did not mean Timothy should keep the flame going by his own human effort. https://www.gotquestions.org/stir-up-the-gift.html
- *Catholic:* The Catholic Encyclopedia reads this verse as ordination. It says Paul reminds Timothy that he was made a bishop by the imposition of St. Paul's hands, and that grace was attached to this external sign and conferred by it. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/11279a.htm . Catholic Answers adds that this grace is something permanent. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/holy-orders . It also cites the verse for holy orders and apostolic succession, holding that ordination imprints an indelible sacramental character. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/the-biblical-evidence-for-apostolic-succession

**v. 7**
- *The word "fear":* Pulpit Commentary: the Greek word means cowardice and only occurs here in the New Testament. https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/1-7.htm . GotQuestions: it isn't the reverent "fear of the Lord" but refers to cowardice or timidity. https://www.gotquestions.org/spirit-of-fear.html
- *"Sound mind":* Ellicott prefers the translation "self-control." https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/1-7.htm . Guzik says the word pictures a calm mind, in contrast to panic. He reads power as love and service, like Jesus washing feet, rather than control over others. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/
- Calvin sees the verse as backing up v. 6, urging Timothy to display the power of the gifts which he had received. Clarke sees an allusion to the giving of the law on mount Sinai. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv2-timothy/1-7.html
- Barnes says this was written because Timothy was not improbably modest and diffident. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt2-timothy/1-7.html
- *Catholic:* this verse shows the ordination grace of v. 6 is a grace which enables Timothy to rightly discharge the office imposed upon him. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/holy-orders

**v. 8**
- Precept Austin quotes Hiebert. In case timid Timothy thought this was beyond him, Paul reminds him the suffering is "according to the power of God." Precept Austin also notes Hebrews 13:23 ("Timothy has been released"), which suggests that Timothy had endured hardship as far as imprisonment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_18-14
- Guzik: following a crucified Master was not easy, and supporting an imprisoned apostle was hard too. Paul calls himself Jesus' prisoner, not Rome's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-timothy-1/

**v. 9**
- Precept Austin: God's "purpose" is His plan, and grace is how He carries it out. Believers were saved and called even before we were born and before He created the world. The reason for salvation did not lie in us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59803

**v. 10**
- Precept Austin: because Christ abolished death, even in the most disturbing times of life, we never need to be scared to death. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_112-14

**v. 12**
- Precept Austin: the Greek perfect tense shows Paul became convinced when he was saved by Christ and he remained convinced of His saving and keeping power. The stress falls on whom Paul knew rather than what he knew. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_112-14 and https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_18-14

**vv. 13–14**
- Precept Austin: Paul means "Timothy don't lose your grip on the standard." The danger is letting go out of fear. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59797/
- Precept Austin quotes MacArthur: truth should be defended in faith and in love, with the right attitude of kindness and compassion toward unbelievers. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59797/
- On "the Holy Spirit who dwells in us," Precept Austin takes a view some Pentecostals would question: every believer has the Spirit - we do not need to pray to receive the Spirit. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/59797/

**v. 15**
- Precept Austin: Paul sets the deserters against loyal Onesiphorus as the vivid contrast between an unfaithful (ashamed) soldier & a faithful (unashamed) soldier. https://www.preceptaustin.org/2_timothy_115-18

**v. 16 (was Onesiphorus dead?)**
- *He had died:* Ellicott says there is little doubt that Onesiphorus had recently died, because mercy is asked for his household and "that day" follows in v. 18. Pulpit Commentary calls this inference undoubtedly probable, though not certain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/1-16.htm
- *He was alive but away:* Barnes says He was himself still living, but probably away from home. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says Nowhere has Paul prayers for the dead. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/2_timothy/1-16.htm

**v. 18 (prayer for the dead: a real Catholic/Orthodox–Protestant difference)**
- *Protestant commentators who deny it:* Barnes says the verse proves that Onesiphorus was then alive, and that there is no evidence he was dead. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/2-timothy/1-18.html . Matthew Henry thinks Onesiphorus was probably with Paul and away from home. He asks, of those who say he was dead, who told them that Onesiphorus was dead? Coffman says that even if he was dead, the words are a prayerful hope, and not as a petition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-18.html
- *Protestant commentators who grant it but limit it:* Ellicott speaks of Paul's "dead friend." He notes Paul's thought pass over the interval between death and judgment. Another commentator on the same page says a pious wish is a very slender foundation for building prayers and Masses for souls in purgatory. https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/1-18.htm . Barclay leaves it open but says many think he had died, and that Paul was brought up in a way of belief which saw in prayers for the dead, not a hateful, but a lovely thing. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/2-timothy/1-18.html
- *Anglican:* A Catholic Answers forum post (a forum, not an official source) quotes Alfred Plummer. He held the verse shows some kinds of intercession for the dead are allowable, but not very different kinds. https://forums.catholic.com/t/prayer-for-the-dead/174259
- *Catholic:* Many scholars have concluded that Onesiphorus had passed away and thus Paul was praying for the departed. https://www.catholic.com/audio/ddp/praying-for-the-dead-2
- *Orthodox:* Fr John Breck calls this the only really clear allusion to such prayer in the New Testament. He says this holds whether or not the letter was penned by the apostle himself. https://www.oca.org/reflections/fr.-john-breck/may-we-pray-for-the-departed
- *What "mercy" means:* Gill: the mercy of Christ to eternal life, the effect of pure grace and mercy, and not of merit. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/2-timothy/1-18.html
- *"Ministered":* Ellicott calls the idea that Onesiphorus was a deacon at Ephesus precarious. https://biblehub.com/2_timothy/1-18.htm
